auditor_firm.note: Not stated in this text dump. Section II (Independent Service Auditor's Assurance Report, pages 6-14) is redacted to 'term-token-...' placeholder lines; no auditor firm name appears anywhere in the extracted text.

report_period.quote: For the Period April 1, 2025 to March 31, 2026

soc2_type.quote: System and Organization Controls 2 (SOC 2) Type 2 Report

trust_services_criteria.quote: Description of the Amazon Web Services System Relevant to Security, Availability, Confidentiality, and Privacy

3.1.1.quote: Customers should use encrypted (TLS/SSL) connections for all of their interactions with AWS. Leading practices include the use of TLS 1.2.

supporting_quotes.quote: All of the AWS APIs are available via TLS/SSL-protected endpoints, which provide server authentication.

AWS KMS endpoints are only accessible via TLS using the following cipher suites that support forward secrecy (Control AWSCA-4.9): TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256

3.1.1.notes: The report states all AWS APIs are TLS/SSL-protected but only names TLS 1.2 explicitly (as leading practice, a customer-responsibility line). The KMS endpoint cipher-suite list on page 67 includes TLS 1.3 suites (TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 etc.) and a PQ-TLS-1-2 policy, so TLS 1.3 is supported on KMS endpoints, but the report never states 'TLS 1.3' as the general standard.

3.1.2.quote: Amazon S3 server-side encryption utilizes 256-bit Advanced Encryption Standard Galois/Counter Mode (AES-GCM) to encrypt all uploaded objects.

supporting_quotes.quote: Data keys provisioned by AWS KMS are encrypted with a 256-bit key unique to the customer's account under a defined mode of AES – Advanced Encryption Standard (Control AWSCA-4.7).

3.1.2.notes: 256-bit AES is stated for S3 server-side encryption and for AWS KMS data-key protection; the report does not make a single blanket at-rest statement covering every service.

3.1.4.quote: Data keys provisioned by AWS KMS are encrypted with a 256-bit key unique to the customer's account under a defined mode of AES – Advanced Encryption Standard (Control AWSCA-4.7).

supporting_quotes.quote: AWS Key Management Service (KMS) allows users to create and manage cryptographic keys. One class of keys, KMS keys, are designed to never be exposed in plaintext outside the service.
KMS will generate an associated key ID if a customer chooses to import their own key.
AWS CloudHSM allows customers to store and use encryption keys within HSMs in AWS data centers.

3.1.4.notes: BYOK is supported (customer key import into KMS, p66) and customer-held keys via CloudHSM (p59); S3 also supports customer-provided keys (SSE-C, p36). Default KMS keys are generated by AWS per customer account.

3.1.8.line: Least-privilege access management for AWS personnel
3.1.8.quote: AWS employs the concept of least privilege, allowing only the necessary access for users to accomplish their job function. User accounts are created to have minimal access.

3.1.8.line: Quarterly vulnerability scanning of the AWS environment
3.1.8.quote: AWS Security performs at least quarterly vulnerability scans on host operating systems, web applications, and databases in the AWS environment using a variety of tools (Control AWSCA-3.4).

3.1.8.line: Application security review and penetration testing
3.1.8.quote: The Application Security team provides their final approval for launch only upon completion of the review (Control AWSCA-3.6). Penetration testing is performed as needed.

3.1.8.line: Network traffic control via virtual networking, host-based firewalls, and ACLs
3.1.8.quote: AWS utilizes virtualization techniques to control and restrict traffic flow. This includes the use of virtual networking devices, host-based firewalls, and Access Control Lists (ACLs) within EC2 and VPC.

3.1.8.line: Data-center physical security: perimeter controls, video surveillance, intrusion detection, MFA to data center floors
3.1.8.quote: Physical access is controlled both at the perimeter and at building ingress points by professional security staff utilizing video surveillance, intrusion detection systems, and badge and pin electronic means. Authorized staff utilize multi-factor authentication mechanisms.

3.1.8.line: MFA required for logging/monitoring tool administration
3.1.8.quote: access and management of the logging and monitoring functionalities required multi-factor authentication.

3.2.1.quote: England: Europe (London) (eu-west-2); France: Europe (Paris) (eu-west-3); Germany: Europe (Frankfurt) (eu-central-1); Ireland: Europe (Ireland) (eu-west-1); Italy: Europe (Milan) (eu-south-1)
3.2.1.notes: In-scope data center regions also include Spain (eu-south-2), Sweden (eu-north-1), Switzerland (eu-central-2) on page 20. EU data-center presence is stated; the report does not itself describe an 'EU Access' contractual program.

absent_notes.3.1.3: The report describes AWS Backup as a service and states authoritative backups of critical AWS system components are maintained (pp. 30, 80), but never states an encryption standard for backups.
absent_notes.3.1.6: No general anonymization capability is stated. Only a service-specific line: 'Amazon Braket anonymizes the content, so that only content necessary to process the quantum task is sent to the quantum hardware provider' (p. 37).
absent_notes.3.1.7: No mention of pseudonymization anywhere in the report text.
